name: Rubefacient

lead: Rubefacients are creams, gels and liniments that make skin red and warm by increasing blood flow where they are applied. Common ingredients include methyl salicylate, nicotinate esters, menthol and capsaicin.

The appearance links are indirect or short-lived: easing muscle and joint discomfort so someone can keep training, and a temporary flush of colour. Trial research is mostly on musculoskeletal pain, where a Cochrane review examined salicylate-containing products.

paras: Users spread a rub over the sore area or skin and feel warmth within minutes. Some warming rubs are used around training sessions. Nicotinate esters are also used in clinical settings to boost local blood flow.
Skin irritation and allergic reactions occur, and salicylate rubs can be absorbed systemically if used on large areas or damaged skin. Product labels advise avoiding broken skin and eyes.

chain: Warmth and soreness relief at the site
Easier training; temporary flush of colour
angle.text: Rubefacients warm and redden the skin. Lifters use them for joint and muscle comfort around training, and the flush gives a short-lived ruddy tone.

lead: A rubefacient is a topical substance that reddens the skin by dilating small blood vessels and increasing local blood flow [1]. Medicinal examples include salicylates such as methyl salicylate, nicotinate esters, capsaicin, menthol and isopropanol; herbal ones include ginger, mustard, garlic and peppermint [1].

People use them mainly as warming rubs for muscle and joint soreness, which supports consistent training and so the physique people build. A second, small appearance use is the temporary pink flush the product produces on skin.

A Cochrane review of topical rubefacients for acute and chronic musculoskeletal pain examined randomised trials of salicylate and nicotinate products [2]. A forum thread on T Nation asks whether methyl salicylate works for joint pain, showing how lifters raise it [3].
infobox: Methyl salicylate, nicotinate esters, menthol, capsaicin [1]

paras: Rubefacients have long been applied for acute and chronic musculoskeletal pain [1][2]. Researchers have also used rubefacient ointments to arterialise the ear for oximetry [4] and benzyl nicotinate to raise skin oxygen levels in measurement studies [5].
Irritation of sensory nerve endings triggers local vasodilation, producing redness and warmth [1]. Capsaicin acts through TRPV1 receptors and causes irritation without redness [1].

The 2009 Cochrane review pooled randomised double-blind trials of salicylate and nicotinamide rubefacients in adults with musculoskeletal pain [2]. A 2014 systematic review of over-the-counter treatments for acute low back pain included a topical rubefacient among thirteen trials [6]. A 1978 randomised trial found a rubefacient ointment improved ear oximeter accuracy in 51 cardiac surgery patients [4].
Reported effects include skin irritation and allergic reactions; salicylate absorption can occur over large areas or broken skin [7]. A rabbit-skin study examined the effect of Tiger Balm [8].

timeline.event: First recorded English use of the word rubefacient, per Grokipedia [7].
